items.title: Catching an AI Scammer
items.summary: Your coworkers are fake and your boss is a voice clone trying to rob you. When a scammer cloned the Ferrari CEO's voice to demand a transfer, an executive stopped the attack cold by asking about a specific book. The scammer was exposed and they avoided tragedy. Arup was not as fortunate. An employee joined a video call packed with fake colleagues and wired away $25.6 million. Deepfakes can replicate a voice and face perfectly. The only real defense left is reaching for a shared memory that a machine cannot scrape from the internet. A voice match is simply no longer enough to prove a caller is human.

items.title: 10,000 AI Experiments in One Weekend
items.summary: In episode 1037 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Richard Socher, CEO of Recursive how AI has changed the way he does his own research. Socher explains that he used to do research mostly through other people, who implemented the ideas he discussed with them, while now he discusses ideas directly with an AI that implements them, running 10,000 experiments over a single weekend. He predicts that, with enough agency, we will all become more like National Science Foundation program directors, collaborating with our AIs to invent the changes we want to see in the world.

items.title: Does Kimi K3.1 Pro Replaces Opus 5.5? (Full Comparison)
items.summary: Kimi K3.1 Pro vs Claude Opus 5.5 on 13 long-horizon agentic coding tasks. Both models ran in the same Claude Code harness, with the same prompts, the same effort setting and the same grading scripts. Only the model string changed. Kimi K3.1 Pro is listed at half the price of Opus 5.5 ($2 / $10 per million input / output tokens vs $4 / $20). Across all 13 tasks it cost $45.91 against Opus's $83.46, about 55% of the bill, and between 28% and 93% depending on the task. The reason is caching: about 98% of everything both models read came from the cache, and cached tokens cost $0.20 per million on both. What I tested: - Research replication: Growing Neural Cellular Automata, PPO from scratch on MuJoCo Ant, a Milky Way and Andromeda collision - 3D in code with no 3D software: an SDF dragon from one concept image, a living planet, a portal physics lab, a mechanical watch - An external tool: two Blender scenes built and refined from Python - Front end: three websites rebuilt from a single screenshot, and a site built to a 33-rule spec Some results: - Ant-v5: Opus 7,435 vs Kimi 5,023 (Opus trained 4x as many steps) - SDF dragon silhouette match: Opus 0.85 / 0.82 vs Kimi 0.65 / 0.62 - Galaxy: Kimi picked the approximate method, and its angular momentum changed by 31.85% - Blender reading room: Kimi's image is the stronger one in my view, at 77% of Opus's cost - 33-rule brief: Opus passed 33/33; Kimi passed 31/33 but reported 33/33 Chapters: 0:00 Kimi K3.1 Pro vs Opus 5.5 1:23 What a long-horizon task is 2:00 The four task groups 2:27 Setup: same Claude Code, only the model changes 3:22 Research: Growing Neural Cellular Automata 4:36 Reinforcement learning: Ant vs HalfCheetah 5:42 Ant vs Ant rematch 6:46 Galaxy collision and energy conservation 8:35 3D in code: the SDF dragon 10:18 WebGL worlds: planet, portal and watch 11:39 Why Kimi took 3-4x longer on 3D 13:16 Blender: reading room and keyboard 15:54 Front end: websites from one screenshot 16:58 The 33-rule brief and the false 33/33 18:28 The real cost of all 13 tasks 19:36 Why half price is not half the bill: caching 21:58 Caveats 22:57 Four rules for using Kimi K3.1 Pro in Claude Code Credits: - SDF dragon experiment: Keenan Crane. Concept art: Inigo Quilez (CC0). - Growing Neural Cellular Automata: Mordvintsev et al., Distill 2020. https://distill.pub/2020/growing-ca/ - Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing: https://platform.kimi.ai Gemini 4 Argon on many of the same tasks: https://youtu.be/yksrd5uNxcw #Kimi #ClaudeCode #AIcoding
items.summary_html:
Kimi K3.1 Pro vs Claude Opus 5.5 on 13 long-horizon agentic coding tasks. Both models ran in the same Claude Code harness, with the same prompts, the same effort setting and the same grading scripts. Only the model string changed.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is listed at half the price of Opus 5.5 ($2 / $10 per million input / output tokens vs $4 / $20). Across all 13 tasks it cost $45.91 against Opus's $83.46, about 55% of the bill, and between 28% and 93% depending on the task. The reason is caching: about 98% of everything both models read came from the cache, and cached tokens cost $0.20 per million on both.

What I tested:
- Research replication: Growing Neural Cellular Automata, PPO from scratch on MuJoCo Ant, a Milky Way and Andromeda collision
- 3D in code with no 3D software: an SDF dragon from one concept image, a living planet, a portal physics lab, a mechanical watch
- An external tool: two Blender scenes built and refined from Python
- Front end: three websites rebuilt from a single screenshot, and a site built to a 33-rule spec

Some results:
- Ant-v5: Opus 7,435 vs Kimi 5,023 (Opus trained 4x as many steps)
- SDF dragon silhouette match: Opus 0.85 / 0.82 vs Kimi 0.65 / 0.62
- Galaxy: Kimi picked the approximate method, and its angular momentum changed by 31.85%
- Blender reading room: Kimi's image is the stronger one in my view, at 77% of Opus's cost
- 33-rule brief: Opus passed 33/33; Kimi passed 31/33 but reported 33/33

items.title: How C-DAC Plans To Build India's Own GPU, CPU And Exaflop Supercomputer By 2032
items.summary: India's push for technological self-reliance (Atmanirbhar Bharat) is expanding from IT services to full-stack sovereign hardware, encompassing indigenous GPU chip designs, exaflop-scale supercomputing clusters, and quantum key distribution networks. Following a record 100 student chip tape-outs in a single year under the Chip-to-Startup (C2S) and Design Linked Incentive (DLI) initiatives, C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing) is scaling sovereign hardware IP to reduce external component dependencies. In this exclusive walkthrough and interview, Senior Tech Journalist Siddharth Jindal tours C-DAC Bangalore with Dr. S.D. Sudarsan, Executive Director of C-DAC Bangalore. Dr. Sudarsan provides a tour of the PARAM Utkarsh supercomputer and the historic PARAM Padma rack, breaks down the PRITI FPGA chip prototyping platform (supporting 2.4 billion digital gates), outlines C-DAC's roadmap for an indigenous GPU demonstration chip and 2032 exaflop cluster, details the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM 2.0), and highlights the upcoming Bengaluru-to-Chennai Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) fiber link. How will indigenous GPU designs and sovereign HPC clusters shape the future of India's deep-tech hardware ecosystem?
